title: Washington State
description: America's second largest wine state: an irrigated desert east of the Cascades with ripe fruit and fresh acidity.
L: Washington is the second largest wine-producing US state, after California, with about 24,000 hectares. Almost all vineyards lie east of the Cascade Mountains, far from rainy Seattle. The Columbia Valley AVA covers about a third of the state and contains most other AVAs, like Yakima Valley, Walla Walla Valley and Red Mountain.

The Cascades block Pacific rain, so eastern Washington is a desert or semi-desert, with as little as 150 to 200 mm of rain a year. Summers are hot and long, with up to 17 hours of daylight at about 46 degrees north. Nights are cool. Irrigation from the Columbia, Yakima and Snake rivers makes vineyards possible.
Why is eastern Washington so dry?
The Cascade Mountains block Pacific rain

Washington's wine industry is young. In 1969, Chateau Ste. Michelle and Columbia Winery began serious winemaking. From about 20 wineries in 1981, there are now over 1,000. Walla Walla, Woodinville, near Seattle, where many wineries have tasting rooms, and the Yakima Valley are centres.
Most Washington vineyards are near rainy Seattle.
Not true. Almost all are east of the Cascades, in a dry desert.
Washington is America's second largest wine state
The Cascades create a desert east of the mountains
Its industry has grown fast since the 1970s

Cabernet Sauvignon is the most planted grape, giving ripe blackcurrant with firm structure and fresh acidity. Merlot, an early success, gives plush, structured wines. Syrah thrives, especially in Walla Walla and Yakima. Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Grenache also grow. Bordeaux-style blends are common.

Chardonnay is the most planted white; Riesling is a speciality, from dry to sweet, made in large volume by Chateau Ste. Michelle, one of the world's largest Riesling producers. The common thread: long, sunny days give ripe fruit; cool nights keep acidity. Washington wines are often described as between Napa ripeness and Bordeaux freshness.
Match each grape to its role.
Washington grows both reds and whites.
Washington Merlot is often more structured than California's, with fresh acidity and firm tannins, a good place to rediscover the grape.
What gives Washington wines ripe fruit and fresh acidity?
Long sunny days and cool nights
Cabernet, Merlot and Syrah lead the reds
Riesling and Chardonnay lead the whites
Long days and cool nights give ripe, fresh wines

Without irrigation, most of eastern Washington couldn't grow vines. Water from rivers and the Cascades' snowmelt is applied by drip, giving growers precise control. Mild water stress can be managed to keep berries small and concentrated. The desert air also limits disease, so fewer sprays are needed.

Soils are mostly wind-blown loess and sand, over basalt, left by the Missoula Floods at the end of the last ice age. Phylloxera struggles in sand, so most vines are planted on their own roots. The main risk is winter cold: temperatures can drop below minus 20 degrees, killing vines. Growers plant on slopes for air drainage.
Why are most Washington vines own-rooted?

Washington has 20 AVAs. Red Mountain, small and warm, gives powerful Cabernet. Walla Walla Valley, straddling Oregon, gives Syrah and Cabernet; its Rocks District, of cobblestones, is famous for savoury Syrah. Yakima Valley, the oldest AVA, from 1983, grows many grapes. Horse Heaven Hills, near the Columbia, is large and windy.
Drip irrigation makes Washington's desert vineyards possible
Sandy soils let vines grow on their own roots
Red Mountain, Walla Walla and Yakima are key AVAs
Reading Washington and eating with it

Labels show the winery, grape, AVA and vintage. Washington uses US federal rules for AVAs, 85%, and vintage, 95%, but requires 85% for a named grape, stricter than the federal 75%. Columbia Valley is the broadest AVA; Red Mountain or Walla Walla are more specific. Many wineries are in Woodinville but source grapes from the east.

Washington Cabernet suits steak, lamb and burgers; Merlot suits roast pork and duck; Syrah suits barbecue, lamb and game; Riesling suits Asian food, seafood and spicy dishes. Pacific Northwest salmon suits lighter reds and Chardonnay. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees, Riesling at 7 to 10.
Cabernet with steak, Riesling with spice
Which Washington AVA is famous for savoury Syrah from cobblestones?
Woodinville, near Seattle, has over 100 tasting rooms, but most grapes are grown three to four hours east, across the Cascades.
Washington requires 85% of a named grape on the label.
Labels follow 85% rules for grape and AVA
Cabernet suits steak; Syrah suits barbecue; Riesling suits spice
